newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks seen lower, housing starts could help.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks seen lower, housing starts could help.

text.p: U.S. stocks are expected to open weaker on Tuesday morning although data on housing starts, due before the opening bell, could lend strength to the bond and stock markets.
Analysts see the market contining its slight pause after its recent ferocious bull run. Yesterday, stocks snapped their eight- day winning streak and closed down one to about 6345.
The long bond was up 2/32 to yield 6.46 percent and Standard & Poor's December futures were off 0.55 to 739.8, indicating a slightly lower opening.
"I expect a mixed to soft opening, but then we should quickly work lower," said Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood.

At 0830 EST/1330 GMT, the Commerce Department will release October housing starts. U.S. economists in a Reuters survey expect a total of 1.443 million units compared to 1.438 million units in September. Analysts said bonds would benefit if the numbers support a slowdown in the housing market, which could lend support to stocks at the opening.
At 0900 EST/1400 GMT, BTM/Schroders releases weekly chain store sales. In the previous week, sales rose 0.4 percent and in later, the Lynch, Jones & Ryan Inc Redbook retail sales index is due.
"Even if (the numbers) they confirm a slowing economy, the main reason I expect the market to go down today is technical. It needs to take a pause, it's been extraordinary," he said.
An $18.25 billion auction of two-year notes later today could pressure bonds and keep a lid on stock prices.
Hewlett-Packard's soft earnings could "put a damper on the technology stocks today," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.

Hewlett-Packard Co posted fourth quarter earnings slightly below expectations after the bell on Monday. Profits fell 4.0 percent from a year earlier, to $0.62 a share and the computer maker expects margins to remain under pressure.
"We finally got a one day pullback yesterday, breaking the streak, and I expect something of a repeat with some intraday profit-taking," he said.
Tokyo stocks closed higher with the Nikkei-225 share index gaining almost 160 to close at 20,956. London's FTSE 100 index was just a whisper higher, up 0.3 to 3962.4.
The dollar was firm against the mark but lower against the yen in European trading.
The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column says perhaps Thomas Rattigan, a corporate turnaround expert, should run RJR Nabisco.
